title: GOD SHATTERED THEIR UNITY AT BABEL… BUT WHY? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN HUMANITY TRIES TO REACH HEAVEN WITHOUT HIM
paragraphs: GOD SHATTERED THEIR UNITY AT BABEL… BUT WHY? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN HUMANITY TRIES TO REACH HEAVEN WITHOUT HIM

They spoke one language. They shared one vision. They were building something extraordinary. Then God came down and scattered them. Was their unity becoming dangerous—or was something far more disturbing happening inside the human heart? The answer in Genesis 11 may expose something about your own life that you never expected.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning and discovering that the person sleeping beside you no longer understands a single word you say.
Your children are crying, but their words sound foreign.
Your closest friend is standing in front of you, desperately trying to explain something, but nothing makes sense.
Yesterday, everyone understood one another.
Today, the world has become a thousand conversations that cannot connect.
Now imagine that this wasn't an accident.
God Himself had intervened.
Not because humanity was fighting.
Not because nations were at war.
Not because people couldn't cooperate.
But at the very moment humanity had achieved something we still struggle to accomplish today.
Unity.
One language. One people. One enormous ambition.
And God stopped them.
Why?
Was God threatened by human progress?
Was He afraid of what humanity could accomplish?
Was unity itself becoming dangerous?
Or was God seeing something beneath their impressive civilization that human eyes could never recognize?
Because here's what makes the Tower of Babel so unsettling.
The people weren't trying to destroy the world. They were trying to build something great.
And that should make every one of us pay attention.
Especially those of us who have spent our lives building something, achieving something, proving something, or desperately trying to become somebody.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing in your life isn't the sin you're ashamed of.
Sometimes it's the success you're proud of.
And the story of Babel reveals why.
Genesis 11:1 begins with a deceptively peaceful statement:
“And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.” — Genesis 11:1, KJV
In Hebrew, the expression is safah echat u-devarim achadim (שָׂפָה אֶחָת וּדְבָרִים אֲחָדִים).
Literally, it describes one lip or language and unified words or speech.
Humanity possessed something extraordinary: the ability to communicate without the barriers that divide nations today.
No interpreters.
No linguistic misunderstandings.
No translation difficulties.
A shared language made collective achievement possible on an astonishing scale.
And Scripture doesn't describe this shared language as evil.
That matters.
Because God was not condemning communication, cooperation, technological development, or unity simply because they were powerful.
The Bible repeatedly celebrates righteous unity.
Psalm 133:1 declares:
“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”
Jesus Himself prayed that His followers would be one (John 17:20–23).
So the problem at Babel could not have been unity by itself.
The real question is what that unity was serving.
And Genesis gives us the answer.
As the people migrated, they settled on a plain in the land of Shinar.
There, they discovered what could be accomplished when shared ambition met human ingenuity.
Genesis 11:3 records:
“Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly.”
They began using baked bricks and bitumen for mortar.
These weren't helpless, primitive people stumbling through history.
They were builders.
Organizers.
Innovators.
People who understood that cooperation could transform the physical world.
And then came the sentence that exposed the spiritual direction of their civilization.
Genesis 11:4:
“Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.”
Read those words again.
Slowly.
“Let us make us a name.”
There it is.
Not merely a construction project.
Not merely architectural ambition.
A declaration of human self-importance.
In Hebrew, the phrase is na'aseh-lanu shem (נַעֲשֶׂה־לָּנוּ שֵׁם).
It means, “Let us make a name for ourselves.”
They wanted significance.
Security.
Recognition.
A lasting identity built around their own achievements.
And suddenly, this ancient story begins to sound painfully modern.
Because isn't that what so many of us are still doing?
Building a name.
Building a reputation.
Building an empire.
Building a life impressive enough that nobody can question our worth.
We want people to remember us.
We want our accomplishments to prove that we matter.
We want enough money that we never feel vulnerable again.
Enough influence that nobody can overlook us.
Enough recognition that the insecurity buried inside us finally becomes quiet.
And sometimes, even while claiming to believe in God, we begin constructing a life where we no longer feel the need to depend on Him.
We pray for success.
Then slowly allow success to replace prayer.
We ask God to bless our plans.
Then become offended when His direction interrupts them.
We want heaven's approval without surrendering earthly control.
And without realizing it, we begin building our own Babel.
Perhaps yours doesn't have bricks.
Perhaps yours has a business logo.
A beautiful house.
A growing social media following.
An impressive ministry.
A career title.
A bank account.
Or an image of spiritual strength that you're terrified of losing.
And the frightening question is not whether those things are inherently wrong.
Many of them can be good gifts.
The question is whether they have become the foundation of your identity.
Are you building something for God's glory, or are you using God's name to build something for your own?
That question reaches deeper than ancient history.
It reaches into the hidden rooms of the human heart.
And there is another detail in Genesis 11:4 that is easy to overlook.
The people said:
“Lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.”
They weren't simply chasing greatness.
They were resisting dispersion.
Earlier in Genesis, God had blessed humanity with the responsibility to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (Genesis 1:28; 9:1).
But Babel's builders wanted to remain concentrated in one place, unified around one center of human achievement.
Their project was not merely about height.
It was about control.
They wanted to secure their future on their own terms.
They wanted to prevent the very scattering that would spread humanity across the earth.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes what looks like ambition is actually fear wearing expensive clothing.
Sometimes the person working endlessly isn't merely hardworking.
They're terrified of becoming insignificant.
Sometimes the person desperate for recognition isn't simply arrogant.
They're trying to silence the voice that has told them their entire life that they aren't enough.
Sometimes the person controlling everyone around them isn't feeling powerful.
They're afraid of what will happen if they let go.
That doesn't excuse pride or disobedience.
But it helps us recognize how deeply sin can entangle our desires.
We want to be somebody.
We want to belong.
We want to feel secure.
And instead of receiving our identity and security from God, we attempt to manufacture them ourselves.
Babel was a city built with human hands.
But beneath its bricks was an ancient human temptation.
To establish life, identity, and security apart from trusting the Creator.
Then comes one of the most remarkable moments in the entire account.
Genesis 11:5 says:
“And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.”
Did you catch the irony?
They were building a tower whose top was associated with the heavens.
A structure meant to symbolize extraordinary human greatness.
And yet the biblical narrator says God had to “come down” to see it.
Not because God lacked knowledge.
Not because the tower was physically beyond His sight.
Scripture consistently teaches that God knows all things.
The language is a vivid, human-like description of divine examination and intervention.
The irony is deliberate and devastating.
What humanity considered towering greatness was still infinitely beneath the majesty of God.
They were reaching upward in pride.
But the Lord was never threatened by their height.
He was examining their hearts and the direction of their collective rebellion.
Genesis 11:6 records God's words:
“Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.”
At first glance, that sounds almost frightening.
Was God admitting that humanity had become too powerful?
Could human beings eventually challenge His throne?
Absolutely not.
The God who created the heavens and the earth by His word cannot be overthrown by bricks, technology, political cooperation, or human engineering.
Isaiah 46:9 declares:
“I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me.”
The statement in Genesis 11:6 is not an admission of divine weakness.
It is a sober recognition of what coordinated human determination could accomplish when directed toward a rebellious purpose.
The Hebrew expression translated “imagined to do” comes from the verb zamam (זָמַם), which concerns planning, devising, or intending.
The issue was not that humanity could literally do anything imaginable.
It was that their shared language and organized determination were enabling the pursuit of their chosen course without the ordinary barriers that might slow them down.
Think about that.
Human cooperation is powerful.
But cooperation does not automatically make a purpose righteous.
A crowd can unite around compassion.
Or cruelty.
A nation can organize to protect the vulnerable.
Or persecute them.
A community can build hospitals.
Or construct systems of oppression.
Unity magnifies the direction of the hearts involved.
When people unite around truth, unity can become a blessing. When people unite around rebellion, unity can multiply the damage.
And perhaps that is the most uncomfortable lesson of Babel.
Not every movement deserves your loyalty simply because it is popular.
Not every vision deserves your participation simply because it is impressive.
Not every leader deserves your trust simply because thousands are following.
And not every successful project carries God's approval.
A crowd can be completely united and completely wrong.
The builders of Babel were united.
But their unity did not make their intentions holy.
Then God spoke.
Genesis 11:7:
“Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech.”
The Hebrew verb behind “confound” is balal (בָּלַל), meaning to mix or confuse.
And in the next verses, the narrative connects this confusion with the name Babel.
Genesis 11:9 explains that the place was called Babel because the LORD confused the language of the whole earth there.
The passage uses a Hebrew wordplay between Bavel (בָּבֶל), Babel, and balal, to confuse.
There is an important historical detail here.
The name Babylon is commonly connected linguistically with the Akkadian Bāb-ilim, often understood as “Gate of God.”
Genesis, however, gives a theological wordplay that associates Babel with confusion.
The biblical writer is not simply presenting a modern dictionary definition of the city's name.
He is revealing the theological meaning of what happened there.
Humanity sought a place of greatness.
God made it a place remembered for the failure of self-exalting ambition.
And suddenly, the people who had been able to accomplish extraordinary things together could no longer understand one another.
Imagine the scene.
A builder calls for another brick.
His coworker stares in confusion.
An overseer gives instructions.
The workers exchange frightened looks.
Someone shouts louder.
Someone else responds angrily.
Families try to communicate.
Neighbors search one another's faces for understanding.
The shared words that once held their project together no longer work.
The construction stops.
The community begins to disperse.
And the city that was meant to prevent scattering becomes the place from which the people are scattered.
Genesis 11:8 says:
“So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city.”
The story does not describe exactly how each family reacted or how long the confusion unfolded.
Those human details must remain imaginative possibilities rather than claims about what Scripture explicitly records.
But the outcome is unmistakable.
God interrupted the project.
The city remained unfinished.
And the people were scattered.
Now here is the question that changes how we understand the entire account.
Was this only judgment—or was there also mercy in the interruption?
The text explicitly presents God's action as a response to human ambition and resistance to His purposes.
It does not directly say, “God confused their languages to save them from themselves.”
We should not pretend it does.
Yet within the larger biblical story, we can recognize a merciful dimension in God's restraint of coordinated rebellion.
God did not annihilate humanity at Babel.
He disrupted their project.
He limited what their unified defiance could accomplish.
And humanity continued.
The story ends with scattering, not extinction.
Sometimes God's judgment exposes the emptiness of human pride while His patience leaves room for the unfolding of His redemptive purpose.
That should make us think differently about the things God sometimes allows to collapse in our own lives.
But we must be careful.
Not every failed business is a judgment from God.
Not every broken relationship is evidence of divine punishment.
Not every unexpected setback is God destroying your personal tower.
Scripture does not authorize us to interpret every painful circumstance that way.
Faithfulness requires humility about what God has and has not revealed.
Still, Babel invites a searching question.
What happens when the thing we trust more than God begins to fall apart?
When the career that gave us identity disappears?
When the applause stops?
When the relationship we thought would save us ends?
When the reputation we carefully constructed is shaken?
When the money we believed would make us secure cannot heal the pain inside our home?
Sometimes the collapse exposes what the success concealed.
We discover that we were asking temporary things to carry eternal weight.
And that is a burden they were never created to bear.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from spending years building a life that looks successful to everyone except the person living inside it.
You smile for photographs.
You celebrate milestones.
You tell people how blessed you are.
But when the lights go out and the house becomes quiet, there is still something unsettled in your soul.
Because achievement can fill a résumé without healing a heart.
Recognition can make your name famous without making your spirit whole.
And a thousand people can applaud you while you remain terrified of being forgotten.
Babel asks whether we have mistaken being noticed for being known.
Because God already knows you.
Not merely the polished version.
Not the carefully edited testimony.
Not the public identity you work so hard to maintain.
He knows the envy you hide.
The resentment you justify.
The pride you rename confidence.
The fear beneath your ambition.
The compromises you hope nobody discovers.
And the exhaustion of trying to prove that you deserve to matter.
He sees all of it.
And the Gospel announces something astonishing.
The God who sees your sin is also the God who has provided a Savior for sinners.
But to understand how extraordinary that is, we need to look at what happens immediately after Babel.
Genesis 11 does not end with humanity's failure and leave the story there.
The genealogy that follows leads toward Abram.
And in Genesis 12, God calls Abram and makes a promise.
Genesis 12:2 says:
“And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing.”
Did you notice the contrast?
At Babel, humanity declares:
“Let us make us a name.”
To Abram, God says:
“I will… make thy name great.”
At Babel, people attempt to manufacture greatness for themselves.
In God's covenant promise, greatness is received through divine grace and calling.
And the promise goes even further.
Genesis 12:3 declares:
“And in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.”
All families.
Not merely one city.
Not merely one language.
Not merely one nation.
The same biblical story that records the scattering of humanity begins unfolding God's promise of blessing for the nations.
And the New Testament reveals how that promise reaches its fulfillment.
Through Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:8 connects God's promise to Abraham with the Gospel being announced beforehand.
Galatians 3:14 teaches that the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles through Christ Jesus.
This is not a small detail.
It is the beginning of a breathtaking redemptive movement.
Humanity sought greatness apart from God.
God initiated a promise that would bring blessing to the nations through His chosen Redeemer.
And centuries later, another extraordinary event took place.
In Jerusalem.
On the day of Pentecost.
Acts 2 describes believers being filled with the Holy Spirit and speaking in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.
People from many nations heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their own languages.
Acts 2:6 says:
“Every man heard them speak in his own language.”
Do you see the beauty of that moment?
At Babel, human language became a barrier in the context of rebellious self-exaltation.
At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit enabled the proclamation of God's mighty works across language barriers.
The connection is not presented in Acts as a direct quotation or explicit reversal of Genesis 11.
But the theological contrast is profound.
At Babel, humanity tried to establish greatness through its own unified project.
At Pentecost, God empowered witnesses to proclaim the greatness of Jesus Christ.
At Babel, communication was disrupted.
At Pentecost, people from different nations understood the message of God's works.
And there is something especially important here.
Pentecost did not require everyone to abandon their native language and become culturally identical.
The miracle was that people heard the message in their own languages.
God's redemptive purpose does not require every nation to lose its identity.
The Gospel crosses boundaries without demanding that every culture become the same.
Jesus is not merely the Savior of one language group.
He is the Savior proclaimed to the nations.
And one day, Scripture gives us a glimpse of the ultimate destination of that redemption.
Revelation 7:9 describes:
“A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues.”
They stand before the throne and before the Lamb.
Different peoples.
Different languages.
One redeemed multitude worshiping the same Savior.
This is the unity Babel could never produce.
Not because language differences are inherently sinful.
Not because diversity is a curse that must be erased.
But because humanity's deepest division cannot be healed merely by giving everyone the same vocabulary.
Our deepest problem is sin.
And our deepest need is reconciliation with God.
The solution is not another tower.
The solution is Jesus Christ.
And now we arrive at the part of the story that should bring every proud human heart to silence.
Because there is another astonishing contrast between Babel and the Gospel.
At Babel, humanity wanted to reach heaven through its own construction.
In the Gospel, the eternal Son of God came from heaven to dwell among us.
John 1:14 declares:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
The Greek expression ho Logos sarx egeneto (ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο) means “the Word became flesh.”
This is the wonder of the incarnation.
The eternal Word did not merely send humanity another set of architectural instructions for reaching God.
He entered our human condition.
He lived among us.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He revealed God's truth.
And He went to the cross.
At Babel, people sought to make their own name great.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ's humility.
Though truly divine, He took the form of a servant, became human, and humbled Himself in obedience unto death—even death on a cross.
Human pride says, “Let me rise above everyone.”
Christlike humility says, “Let me serve.”
Human pride says, “Let the world recognize my greatness.”
Jesus declared in Mark 10:45 that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
And that is where the Gospel confronts us.
Because our problem is not merely that we sometimes build the wrong things.
Our problem is that sin has distorted the very center of our hearts.
We want God's gifts without God's authority.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
We want spiritual comfort without surrender.
We want Jesus to rescue us from consequences while leaving our idols untouched.
But Christ did not die merely to improve the appearance of our towers.
He died to redeem sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we had finally become impressive.
Not when our reputations were spotless.
Not when we had achieved enough to deserve heaven.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And He rose again.
His resurrection is not a symbolic reminder that things sometimes get better.
It is God's decisive victory through Christ over death, and the foundation of the Christian hope of resurrection and eternal life.
First Corinthians 15:3–4 places Christ's death for our sins, His burial, and His resurrection on the third day at the heart of the Gospel.
The answer to Babel is not that humanity must become more impressive.
The answer is that humanity needs a Redeemer.
And His name is Jesus.
Perhaps you've spent years trying to make yourself worthy of love.
Perhaps you grew up believing that if you became successful enough, nobody would ever abandon you.
Perhaps your entire life has been a desperate attempt to prove something to people who wounded you.
Or perhaps your Babel is religious.
You serve.
You attend church.
You quote Scripture.
You post Christian messages.
You know how to sound spiritually mature.
But deep inside, you know there are areas of your life where you have refused to let Christ rule.
You want the appearance of surrender without the cost of obedience.
You want to be associated with Jesus while still occupying the throne of your own heart.
And now the words of Christ confront you.
Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
Not build a platform around yourself.
Not protect your pride at any cost.
Not negotiate obedience whenever it becomes uncomfortable.
Deny yourself.
Take up your cross daily.
Follow Him.
That is not a call to self-hatred.
It is a call to abandon self-rule and entrust your life to the Savior who gave Himself for you.
And there is grace here for the person who recognizes that they have been building the wrong kingdom.
You do not need to pretend that your tower is still standing.
You do not need to keep defending the decisions that are destroying your peace.
You do not need to hide behind the image of someone who has everything under control.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can come to Christ.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to continue living comfortably in rebellion.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs more than another motivational message.
Not another promise that their dreams will become reality.
Not another declaration that every obstacle will disappear.
But the courage to say:
“Lord, I've been building a life around myself.”
“I've wanted people to admire me more than I've wanted You to transform me.”
“I've been afraid to surrender because I thought surrender meant losing everything.”
“Forgive me.”
“Teach me to build what honors You.”
“Teach me to trust You even when I cannot control the outcome.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
If that prayer expresses what is happening in your heart, don't bury it beneath another distraction.
Respond to God sincerely.
Not because a comment can save you.
Only Christ saves.
Not because public words replace private repentance.
They never can.
But because sometimes an honest confession can encourage another exhausted believer to stop pretending.
There is no shame in asking fellow believers to pray.
We were never commanded to carry every burden alone.
There is another truth we cannot afford to miss.
Babel reminds us that impressive things can be built for the wrong reasons.
And that warning applies even to Christian ministry.
A church can become obsessed with numbers while neglecting discipleship.
A ministry can become consumed with visibility while forgetting humility.
A Christian creator can begin measuring spiritual significance by likes, shares, followers, and financial support.
And a good mission can become distorted when recognition becomes more important than faithfulness.
We must never confuse reach with righteousness.
Or popularity with God's approval.
Or financial growth with spiritual fruit.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“For without me ye can do nothing.”
That is a sobering word for everyone who serves in His name.
Including us at Gospel Warrior.
We don't want to build another Babel with Christian branding.
We want to point people to Christ.
We want Scripture to remain central.
We want the wounded to encounter the hope of the Gospel, the wandering to hear the call to repentance, and believers to be strengthened in biblical truth.
We want people to remember Jesus long after they have forgotten who wrote the article.
And if this message has helped you see your own life more clearly, you can help it reach someone who may be quietly building a tower of fear, pride, or desperation.
Not simply to increase its visibility, but because someone among your friends may be exhausted from trying to prove their worth.
Someone may be succeeding publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone may have stopped praying because they believe they've gone too far from God.
Someone may need to be reminded that grace is still available through Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not to create a crowd that admires us.
It is to help people become disciples who love and follow Jesus.
There is also a practical way to help sustain and expand this work.
It cannot purchase forgiveness, guarantee blessings, or make you more acceptable to Christ.
And it is not a biblical requirement for proving that you glorify God.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But voluntary generosity can be a meaningful way to support the proclamation of the Gospel and the spiritual nourishment of others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But willing partnership in a mission you believe is worth supporting.

Your voluntary support can help sustain the creation of Scripture-centered articles, Christian teaching, discipleship resources, and outreach to readers who may never enter a church building on their own.
And we want to express our appreciation in a practical way.
These products are not the reason to follow Christ, and no purchase can replace a living relationship with Him.
They are simply an added thank-you to those helping sustain the work.
And the Gospel must never be turned into something people have to purchase.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Everything else is simply an opportunity to serve Him faithfully.
Now, before you leave this story, return with me one final time to that ancient plain in Shinar.
Picture the unfinished city.
The abandoned construction.
The bricks that were meant to secure a civilization's greatness.
The tower that was supposed to make humanity unforgettable.
The voices that no longer understood one another.
And the dream that could no longer continue.
They wanted to make a name that would endure.
But the name that endured was Babel.
A reminder of confusion.
A warning about pride.
A testimony to the limits of human ambition when it refuses to submit to God.
And yet the Bible does not end with Babel.
It moves toward Abraham.
Toward God's covenant promises.
Toward the prophets.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Pentecost.
And ultimately toward a redeemed multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language worshiping before the throne of God and the Lamb.
What humanity could not accomplish through self-exaltation, God is bringing about through His redemptive work in Jesus Christ.
And that is the breathtaking difference between Babel and the Gospel.
Babel says, “We will make ourselves great.”
The Gospel says, “Christ is Lord.”
Babel says, “We will establish our own security.”
The Gospel calls us to trust the Savior who holds our eternal hope.
Babel says, “We will make a name for ourselves.”
The Gospel declares that there is salvation in no other name than Jesus Christ (Acts 4:12).
And perhaps the most important question you can ask tonight is not whether God will bless everything you are building.
It is whether what you are building is rooted in obedience to Him.
Because one day, the applause will fade.
The titles will lose their power.
The possessions will pass into other hands.
The platforms will disappear.
And the things that once seemed so enormous will be revealed for what they were.
Temporary.
But Christ remains.
His kingdom remains.
His Word remains.
And those who belong to Him have a hope that death itself cannot destroy.
So don't spend your entire life building a tower that cannot save you.
Come to the Savior who can.
Repent of the pride that has kept you distant.
Receive His grace through faith.
Trust the forgiveness secured by His death and resurrection.
And let your life become a testimony not to how high you managed to climb, but to how mercifully Jesus reached you.
Because the world doesn't need another generation of people who know how to make themselves famous but have forgotten how to kneel before God.
It needs people whose lives bear witness to the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps, years from now, nobody will remember the impressive things you tried to build for yourself.
But someone will remember that you pointed them to Jesus.
Someone will remember that you prayed with them.
Someone will remember that you told them the truth when they were lost.
Someone will remember that you shared the Gospel when they were ready to give up.
And by God's grace, that testimony may outlast every tower you could ever construct.
Because the greatest tragedy isn't watching your tower fall. It's reaching the top of everything you ever wanted—and discovering you built your entire life without the One who could save your soul.
